1:
The ornament under the brim of the sea sets the three against one another, and the question is which history was copied wrong. This text puts figured oxen there; Kings puts wild gourds, which the older English renders knops. Clarke takes the Kings reading for the true one and explains how the error could arise, since two pairs of Hebrew letters are easily confused in old manuscripts, so that grapes might be turned into oxen. He then disposes of a reconciliation he does not accept. Houbigant had argued that both texts are right because the word means a large kind of grape, on Arabic authority; Clarke replies that it has no such sense in Arabic and traces the mistake to a lexicon entry glossing ox-eye as a large black grape used in Palestine for a plum. The criticism of this great man, he concludes, is not solid, and the likeliest reconciliation remains the change of letters. Delitzsch reaches the same verdict in a clause, that the differences here are probably the result of orthographical errors in the Chronicle.

Ellicott refuses the approach entirely. Most commentators assume this text is corrupt and should be restored from Kings, but he sees no reason why the rows round the great basin should not have carried both, small figures of oxen as well as gourds. Reuss objected that oxen ten to the cubit would be absurdly small; Ellicott answers that such work was not beyond the resources of ancient art, and points to the reliefs on the bronze doors of Shalmaneser. He then turns the suspicion the other way: the word for gourds occurs in only one other place in Kings, and a copyist might have repeated it inadvertently from there. To assert that the copyists here have absurdly changed the gourds into oxen is, he says, sheer dogmatism. He notes besides that the Syriac and Arabic omit the verse while the Greek and Latin have it.

The capacity divides them the same way, Kings giving the sea two thousand baths and this text three thousand. Clarke offers a historical rather than a textual solution: the book was written after the captivity, so the measure may be the Babylonish bath, which could have been smaller, exactly as the ancient Hebrew cubit was longer than the Babylonish by a palm; and the Targum, he reports, cuts the knot by making it three thousand of dry measure and two thousand of liquid. Ellicott weighs two scribal accidents and prefers the one that puts the fault in Kings: a copyist might have read the indefinite word for thousands as the dual two thousand and then supplied three from the previous verse, but it is likelier that three was dropped from Kings and the vague thousands made definite, either slip being possible since in the unpointed text the two are written alike. Delitzsch again ascribes the difference to orthography, and declines a further emendation: a verb here looks superfluous and has been called a gloss imported from Kings, but the expression is merely pleonastic and there is no sufficient reason to strike it out.

At the lavers they divide by interest rather than verdict. Clarke states the use plainly, that the lavers served for washing the parts of the victims while the sea was for the priests, who bathed in it or drew water from it. Ellicott observes that the writer returns to his abbreviating style and omits the ten wheeled stands which Kings describes in full and curious detail, guessing that he thought them less important than the furniture described next, or that the difficulty of the passage decided him; and he notes that the statement about washing in them is peculiar to this writer while their size and capacity are given only in Kings. Delitzsch supplies what this text omits, that the lavers stood on ten brazen stands, chests provided with carriage wheels.
7:
Delitzsch opens on the structural oddity of this stretch. These verses are simply not in the parallel narrative, where the note on the position of the brazen sea follows straight after the stands and the lavers; the candlesticks and the table of shewbread do appear there in the summary catalogue, and the inner court in the description of the building, but the outer court is never expressly mentioned. He can give no reason for the omission, and concludes only that the verses must have dropped out rather than never been written. Ellicott makes the same point from the other side: the ten tables are absent from the parallel, which speaks of one table only, and although bowls are mentioned there no number is given.

On the form of the candlesticks two witnesses agree and a third reading is set aside. Ellicott renders the phrase as according to their rule or prescribed manner, supporting it from the Latin and from the Syriac and Arabic, which have according to their laws; the explanation that it means as their use required he judges less likely. Wesley says the same thing in a line, that the form meant is the old form God prescribed to Moses. Ellicott adds a correction to the next clause, that the lampstands were set not in the temple but before the chancel.

What the ten tables were for produces a flat contradiction. Ellicott suggests the golden candelabra perhaps stood upon them. Delitzsch denies precisely that, attributing the idea to a critic he names and answering that the tables were not to bear the candlesticks but were for the shewbread, as the later verse shows. Wesley takes the shewbread reading too and draws an inference from the number: the tables were those on which the shewbread was set, perhaps each of them holding twelve loaves, so that as the house was enlarged the provision was enlarged with it.

The hundred basons bring the three into agreement against another rejected reading. Clarke calls them a sort of sacrificial spoons with which libations were made. Ellicott makes them bowls for pouring libations and cites the prophet in whose book the word occurs. Delitzsch rules out the alternative explicitly: not vessels for catching and sprinkling the blood, as the same critic had held, but wine flagons, their connection with the tables of shewbread showing as much, and the meaning put beyond doubt by that same passage in the prophet. Ellicott notes besides that the Syriac and Arabic put the number of these vessels at a hundred and twenty.

The two courts are identified alike by everyone and described by almost nobody. Clarke gives it in two clauses, the court of the priests being the inner and the great court the outer, or the place where the people assembled. Delitzsch observes that neither is further described, and that the only remark made about the outer court is that it had doors whose leaves were overlaid with copper. Ellicott adds the philology and the archaeology. The word for the outer court is a late one, common in the Targums, standing where the older classical term had just been used, and the court is not mentioned at all in the parallel; the Greek calls it the great court and the Latin the great basilica, while the Syriac rewrites the verse into a single court for priests and Levites with doors and bolts covered in bronze. On the plating he supplies a measure from the spade: the bronze-plated doors of the palace at Balawat stood twenty-two feet high, each leaf six feet wide. On the last verse he reads the Hebrew literally, that the sea was set on the right shoulder, eastward, in front of the southward, that is on the south-east side, and notes that the Greek and some manuscripts add the words of the house, which appear to have fallen out.
11:
What it means to call the craftsman Huram his father is explained three ways that lean on one another. Clarke makes it a title of office, the Hebrew word being often used of a master or chief operator, and reports the Chaldee rendering it so, that all these Chiram his master made for the king. Wesley makes it a title of respect, Solomon calling him so out of regard for his excellent art and service, it being usual to call great artists by such a name. Henry supplies the provenance that makes both work: probably a nickname, Father Huram, since the king of Tyre had called him my father, in compliance with which Solomon called him his, he being the father of the artificers in brass and iron.

Henry draws two observations from the summary. The workman was punctual, finishing all he was to make and leaving no part undone. The king was generous, making the vessels in great abundance, many of a sort, so that many hands might be employed, or that some might be laid up against the wearing out of others; and the brass left over he could not turn to his own use, it being devoted to God. Freely he had received, Henry says, and freely he would give. Delitzsch is interested in where the half verse belongs: the heavier copper utensils named here, pots for ashes, shovels for taking them out and basins for the blood, go with what precedes rather than with the catalogue following, which is clear because the same utensils appear again a few verses later.

Ellicott works through the list correcting the English, and twice the question turns on a single letter. Where Kings has lavers this text has pots, and he judges our reading correct, supported by many manuscripts and by the Greek and Latin of Kings, a single stroke making the difference; the pots were scuttles for carrying ashes away. At the bases the repeated verb strikes him as suspicious: the text reads that the bases he made and the lavers he made upon the bases, where the parallel shows the right reading to be the bases ten and the lavers ten upon them, the word for ten closely resembling the words for he made; the Greek renders it the same awkward way, which shows the corruption to be ancient. On the pommels and chapiters he prefers globes and capitals, notes that the English of Kings gives bowls where the Hebrew is identical, and settles what the numeral counts by grammar, since two is feminine and agrees with globes and capitals while pillars is masculine. The wreaths he makes lattices, the word the English of Kings renders network.

Two further notes bear on the making rather than the naming. The fleshhooks should apparently be bowls, but since the law names pots, shovels, bowls and fleshhooks in succession as altar utensils, perhaps both words belong here and in Kings. And he rejects the suggestion that the instruments might be the moulds the vessels were cast in, on the ground that moulds would not be made of polished brass. Clarke is at the same place from the other side, reporting that some suppose the instruments were not cast at the sites named but that the clay was brought from that quarter as the most proper for moulds. On the ground Ellicott reads the Hebrew as the thickness of the earth, the stiff or clayey soil, notes that the word Kings uses occurs nowhere else, and holds the two forms of the place-name to denote one place. He closes with two accounts of the final verse, either a copyist whose eye wandered forward, or the chronicler missing the force of the verb in Kings and substituting an easier term. One other fact he records weighs more than any of these: the Syriac and Arabic omit this whole stretch of the chapter.
19:
The tables of shewbread are where Ellicott charges this writer with an inconsistency he cannot resolve. Here and in two other places he speaks of tables in the plural where Kings mentions one only; yet elsewhere the same writer speaks of the Pure Table and the Table of the Pile as though there were one. The difficulty, Ellicott says, cannot be solved with certainty, but it seems likely that, finding a number of tables in one of his sources, he grouped them with the table of shewbread, gaining brevity at the cost of accuracy; and he notes that eight tables of hewn stone are named elsewhere, on which the victims were slain. Delitzsch registers the same divergence more mildly, that in the enumeration of the golden furniture this text departs further from the parallel than before.

On the candlesticks the two agree about what has been left out and why. Delitzsch notes that the number and position are not given here as in Kings because both had already been stated earlier, and that in their place the use of the lamps is emphasised, that they should be lit according to the rule before the most holy place. Ellicott describes the same exchange from the other side: the clause about the lamps burning according to the legal rule is the chronicler's addition, and the five on the right and five on the left of Kings is what he drops. Wesley glosses the rule in a line, as the prescription God gave to Moses. Clarke alone pictures the thing: probably each branch of the chandelier was made like a plant in flower, the opening of the flower being either the lamp or its support.

The phrase rendered that perfect gold draws the closest attention in the chapter, and both commentators defend it. Ellicott reads it as it was perfection of gold, notes that the intensive plural occurs nowhere else, and settles its derivation against Bishop Wordsworth, taking it from the verb meaning to be finished rather than the similar verb he preferred. The Greek omits the clause; the Latin does not, rendering that all were made of purest gold. This little touch added to heighten the effect, Ellicott says, is quite in the manner of the chronicler and certainly not to be suspected, as a critic he names asserts. Delitzsch comes to the same conclusion from the other side. The addition looks superfluous, since before and after these vessels are said to be of precious gold, and the Greek leaves it out, perhaps because the rare word was unintelligible to the translators; but the words probably mean that even the decorations and lesser utensils were of perfect gold.

On the smaller implements Delitzsch does the inventory. The knives were probably used with the snuffers for cleansing and trimming the candlesticks and lamps; they are absent from the tabernacle utensils but appear here and in Kings and twice again among the temple vessels. Golden forks are named once elsewhere in this book and nowhere else, whereas the tabernacle has only brazen flesh-forks, and those as an appurtenance of the altar of burnt offering.

Clarke closes with a protest about method rather than a comment on the doors, of which he says only that they were overlaid with golden plates of unknown thickness. That everything in the tabernacle and the temple was typical or representative of some excellence of the Gospel may be readily credited, he grants, without going into all the detail produced by the pious author of Solomon's Temple Spiritualized. We can see the general reference and the principles of the great design, he says, though we may not be able to make a particular application of the knops, the flowers, the pomegranates, the tongs and the snuffers to some Gospel doctrine; and such spiritualizing is in most cases weak, silly, religious trifling, ill calculated to produce respect for divine revelation.
